reader.summary: This week in the DR Congo was defined by three converging crises. Former President Joseph Kabila formally joined the AFC/M23 rebel coalition in eastern Congo; Kinshasa denounced the move as a prelude to a 'generalized attack' and warned that Kabila's own political family was fracturing over it. The development raised fresh fears that ongoing peace efforts in the east could unravel. The Ebola outbreak also accelerated sharply. The virus spread to an eighth province bordering Central Africa, the UN warned the epidemic was growing 'exponentially,' and the Africa CDC revealed over $700 million in pledged response funds remained unaccounted for. Fearing contagion, mothers in affected areas skipped vital maternal and pediatric care, prompting authorities to launch an improved vaccination drive in Beni. Diplomatically, tensions flared with Brussels after Belgian police searched the homes of President Tshisekedi's relatives; the DRC presidency then restricted its staff's contact with the Belgian embassy. The government also protested Formula 1's decision to race in neighboring Rwanda. Economically, Congo arrested hundreds of Chinese miners in its copper belt, and a $250 million Mercuria copper deal with a Chinese miner was announced, underscoring how deeply the conflict is intertwined with mineral wealth.

Reporters highlighted the growing role of Erik Prince and private paramilitaries in securing Congo's critical-mineral supply chains.
The DR Congo government publicly protested Formula 1's 'indefensible' decision to hold a Grand Prix in neighboring Rwanda.

display.eli5:
So DR Congo is juggling three big problems at once. Former president Joseph Kabila just joined the rebel group M23 in the east, and the government in Kinshasa is furious, calling it the start of a 'generalized attack.' Meanwhile, the Ebola virus keeps spreading to new areas, and the government cannot find where hundreds of millions of dollars in promised help went. On top of that, Belgium and Congo are in a diplomatic fight because Belgian police searched the homes of people related to the current president.

Here is why it is messy: Kabila used to be president himself, so his joining the rebels feels like the opposition getting a celebrity face. The Ebola thing is bad because families are too scared to take their kids to the hospital, and the money that was supposed to stop the outbreak has not shown up. The Belgium thing is about a corruption case that got very personal for the president's family.

Next week, expect Kinshasa to launch a new military operation in the east as a direct response to Kabila's move. Also, someone in the government or the Africa CDC will go public about where the missing Ebola money is, turning it into a naming-and-shaming moment. The Belgium standoff will probably get louder, with one side summoning the other's ambassador.

The surprise to watch for: Kabila's own political family is already splitting, and Vital Kamerhe, a relative, is publicly disagreeing with him. If that turns into a formal rival faction declaration, it would split the opposition in two and change who is who in Congo's politics entirely.

velocity.summary: Between the two reports the DR Congo agenda deepened and broadened rather than shifting direction. The Ebola crisis moved from a contained eastern-corridor emergency to a wider national and regional threat: the virus crossed into a province bordering the Central African Republic, the UN flagged exponential growth, and the Africa CDC exposed a $700 million funding black hole. On the security front, the MONUSCO withdrawal vote gave way to something far more consequential: former President Kabila formally joining the AFC/M23 rebel coalition, which Kinshasa framed as the prelude to a generalized attack. A diplomacy domain appeared for the first time, with Belgian police searching the homes of Tshisekedi relatives and Kinshasa pulling staff back from the Belgian embassy. The economic thread intensified from announced audit plans to mass arrests of Chinese miners and a $250 million Mercuria copper deal, while private paramilitary involvement in mineral logistics entered the picture. The vivid one-off incidents of the earlier report—the plane crash, Karondwa's murder, the boat capsize—have faded from the headlines. Overall the pace is brisk: multiple high-stakes moves landed within 72 hours, and the crises are now visibly interlocking rather than running in parallel.
